articleTitle: Millimetre and sub-millimetre wave radiometer systems
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Millimetre and Sub-Millimetre Wave Heterodyne Receivers
abstract: Technology in the millimetre wave region of the spectrum has made significant advances. Millimetre wave components, up to 200 GHz, have moved from the laboratory curiosities to space qualified systems with proven performance and reliability. There are now several proposals for systems operating at about 600 GHz and higher frequencies. These advances have been made possible mainly by improvements in mixer manufacturing techniques, the availability of suitable diodes, the development of quasi-optical components and local oscillators. The author looks at total power radiometers, the microwave limb sounder (MLS) and the Earth Observing System MLS.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Millimetre and submillimetre wave heterodyne receivers for atmospheric sounding and radioastronomy
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Millimetre and Sub-Millimetre Wave Heterodyne Receivers
abstract: To prepare the space programs on meteorology and astrophysics, the development of two heterodyne instruments has been supported by the French Space Agency (CNES): a ten channels millimetre wave radiometer for atmospheric sounding; and a balloon-borne observatory (PRONAOS) including a 2 metre telescope associated with a submillimetre heterodyne spectrometer for radioastronomy. This receiver includes a SIS mixer using Nb/AlO/sub x//Nb tunnel junctions operating at 4 K, a 6 GHz IF low-noise cooled preamplifier, a LO quasi-optically injected with a phase locked Gunn oscillator and two cascaded frequency multipliers. Noise temperature as low as 300 K has been obtained; less than 200 K is expected.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: MM-wave receiver front-end mixers: technical complexity, or mistaken complacency?
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Millimetre and Sub-Millimetre Wave Heterodyne Receivers
abstract: Advances in Schottky diode technology are reviewed. Milestones are identified in the pattern of introduction of new configurations of diodes. Their consequences are assessed on the design of two-diode subharmonically and fundamentally pumped balanced mixers. Noise-temperature performance data is reported for such mixers, above 100 GHz. It is shown that such two-diode mixers yield comparable performance and superior reliability, relative to the conventional whisker-contacted single-ended (one diode) mixers. In addition, it is shown that two-diode mixers yield, in effect, simpler MM-wave receiver structures compared to similar receivers with conventional single-ended mixers.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Millimetre and Sub-Millimetre Wave Heterodyne Receivers
abstract: Spacecraft receivers require technologies which combine optimum RF performance with robustness and low mass, while meeting volume constraints. The adaptation to the spacecraft application is most significant in the instrument front-end, comprising antenna, antenna feed, and mixer. The millimetric band from 89 GHz upwards is currently characterised by the use of quasi-optical feeds and subharmonically pumped double sideband mixers. In recognition of the increasing need for ever higher operating frequencies, and the stringent mass/volume constraints associated in particular with spacecraft environments, BAe Space Systems has developed an appropriate set of accurate predictive design aids, which have been verified against hardware. A key front-end component whose design is significantly constrained by the spacecraft environment is the mixer. Subharmonically pumped double planar diodes are robust. Experimental work using air-bridged and solid coupling structures was undertaken, and typical performance parameters produced.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Receiving techniques used in the Queen Mary and Westfield College millimetre wave compact range
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Millimetre and Sub-Millimetre Wave Heterodyne Receivers
abstract: The author describes the various receiver configurations that are used in the QMW millimetre wave compact antenna test range to measure antennas in the frequency range 90-200 GHz. The millimetre wave compact antenna test range (mmCATR) at QMW is a single offset reflector constructed from 18 reflector panels of a design identical to those used in the James Clerk Maxwell radio telescope. The panels, with an RMS surface accuracy of between 10 mu m and 16 mu m, form a single offset CATR with focal length of 5.4 m and a reflector aperture that can contain a 3 m diameter circle. The range is enclosed by an anechoic chamber with a separate anti-chamber containing the transmit feed.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: JCMT receiver A2-a 210-280 GHz SIS receiver
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Millimetre and Sub-Millimetre Wave Heterodyne Receivers
abstract: The most sensitive receivers constructed for short millimetre and sub-millimetre wavelengths use superconductor-insulator-superconductor (SIS) tunnel junctions as the mixing elements. The authors describe the design and performance of a 210-280 GHz SIS heterodyne receiver, which was commissioned on the James Clerk Maxwell Telescope, Hawaii in March 1992. A prototype version of this receiver was tested on the JCMT in May 1992, which was then modified for permanent use on the telescope as a facility instrument.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Nb and NbN junction development for MM-wave mixers
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Millimetre and Sub-Millimetre Wave Heterodyne Receivers
abstract: Within the past few years all-refractory superconductor-insulator-superconductor (SIS) tunnel junctions based on Nb/Al/AlO/sub x//Nb technology have displaced lead alloy devices as the preferred junctions for SIS mixers. There is growing interest in materials with higher superconducting energy gaps. NbN has a high gap ( approximately 3 meV) and higher critical temperature than Nb. Its main drawback, apart from the greater complexity of the material itself, stems from its short superconducting coherence length which results in a decrease in the measured gap voltage in proximity barrier structures, as generally used for Nb-based junctions. For this reason, most recent work has concentrated on the direct deposition of MgO as a tunnel barrier. The authors summarise work on Nb devices for MM-wave mixers and then report recent work performed at Cambridge on the fabrication of high quality NbN device structures.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Quasi-optical techniques for MM-wave heterodyne systems
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Millimetre and Sub-Millimetre Wave Heterodyne Receivers
abstract: This paper is a review of some of the quasi-optical techniques that have been used in the design and development of heterodyne systems at St. Andrews University. In the first section a brief introduction to quasi-optics is given, including free-space isolation. Measurement techniques are then reviewed which are useful in the development of heterodyne systems including impedance and oscillator noise measurements. A number of different examples of the use of quasi-optics in heterodyne systems are then presented including cavity stabilisation techniques to improve the FM noise on oscillators, universal polarisation manipulation, single side-band filters, notch filters, spatial filters and a dual polarisation 94 GHz radar system.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: A 490 GHz SIS receiver for the James Clerk Maxwell Telescope
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Millimetre and Sub-Millimetre Wave Heterodyne Receivers
abstract: The authors report the construction of an superconductor-insulator-superconductor (SIS) tunnel junction heterodyne receiver for use over the frequency range 450 to 500 GHz. The receiver uses a reduced height waveguide mount and Pb alloy tunnel junction as the detecting element and a quintupling multiplier to generate the local oscillator frequency. Preliminary performance measurements made with two different junctions have revealed a total system double sideband noise temperature of 180 K at 460 GHz and 280 K at 490 GHz, measured over a 1 GHz instantaneous IF bandwidth centred at 4 GHz. The system will be installed at the James Clerk Maxwell Telescope, Hawaii, and is intended to be used for the investigation of molecular species existing in the interstellar medium.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Analysis of a quasi-optical coupled slot antenna mixer
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Millimetre and Sub-Millimetre Wave Heterodyne Receivers
abstract: An uniplanar quasi-optical antenna-mixer for millimeter-wave-length applications is described. Quasi-optical mixers combine the functions of antenna and mixer in one unit. They can be integrated on passive radiometer (pushbroom or multispot), for Earth observation. An accurate analysis of the coupled slot antenna is proposed. Both propagation and radiation studies are completed. Experimental results are presented and compared with theory.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: An optical feed for high resolution passive millimetre wave imaging systems
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Millimetre and Sub-Millimetre Wave Heterodyne Receivers
abstract: The authors discuss two methods to improve the spatial resolution of millimetre wave imagers. One employs a large primary aperture, a 1.4 m square primary reflector, and the other enhances the resulting images using superresolution techniques. These later techniques effectively boost the high spatial frequency content in the image, thereby sharpening the perceived antenna far field pattern. It is usual in radar applications to taper the primary aperture distribution in order to suppress sidelobes. Such a distribution if used in millimetre wave imaging would result in a loss of the high spatial frequencies required by the superresolution algorithms. In the first section they show why a rectangular aperture distribution is preferred and how this can be achieved by relaying a uniform feed distribution onto the primary reflector using millimetre wave optics. Such relaying techniques have been demonstrated on their 35 GHz imaging system and the resulting imagery is illustrated in the final section.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: A turn-key total power radiometer for atmospheric research
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Millimetre and Sub-Millimetre Wave Heterodyne Receivers
abstract: A novel 7 channel total power radiometer has been developed for atmospheric research. The radiometer has channels at 20.6 GHz, 31.5 GHz, 150 GHz and 4 channels about 183.3 GHz. It is contained within a weatherproof enclosure and temperature stabilised to better than .002 degC/min. Calibration is achieved using internal hot and cold loads. The cold load uses liquid nitrogen to achieve a low temperature reference and has a minimum operating time of three hours. The antenna views the scene through a radome and can scan +or-45 degrees from boresight. Major features of the radiometer are its use of subharmonic mixers for the high frequency channels and its use of a quasi-optical feed system for reflector illumination and channel demultiplexing. The antenna beams are defined by the feed system allowing the use of a plane reflector for scene and calibration target observation.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>
